row.title: The Child That Went with the Fairies
row.author: Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu

plot_extraction.response_text:
A poor widow, Mary Ryan, lives with her four children near Lisnavoura, a hill believed to be haunted by fairies. One autumn evening, while she is away gathering turf and her eldest daughter Nell tends the house, the three younger children play outside until after sunset.

A magnificent old-fashioned carriage drawn by enormous white horses appears. Its malicious dwarf servants frighten the children, but a beautiful lady inside charms them and chooses five-year-old Billy, a golden-haired boy. She lifts him into the carriage while another sinister woman watches. The lady then distracts Billy’s siblings by dropping apples along the road. When they have followed as far as a crossroads near Lisnavoura, a whirlwind of dust envelops the carriage, which vanishes with Billy inside.

The terrified children return and tell their mother, who searches desperately but finds no trace of him. Over the following months, Billy occasionally appears at the cabin door, smiling and silently beckoning to his siblings, but always disappears when they approach. The visits eventually stop.

Nearly a year and a half after the abduction, Billy returns once before dawn, barefoot, ragged, pale, and starving. He silently warms himself at the dying fire, but flees when his sister awakens. He is never seen again. Neither fairy doctors nor a priest can recover him, and his family mourns him as dead, believing he remains hidden somewhere within haunted Lisnavoura.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story is written in a nineteenth-century antiquarian Gothic mode, combining regional realism, oral folklore and the structure of a cautionary fairy tale. Its atmosphere depends on the close interweaving of an accurately mapped Irish landscape with supernatural belief. Roads, bogs, mountains, ruined castles, cabins and historical place names are described with topographical precision before Lisnavoura is established as a liminal, haunted presence. This slow geographical opening gives the account the air of local history or collected testimony, making the later marvels seem rooted in an actual community rather than in an abstract fantasy world.

The narrative voice is authoritative, retrospective and occasionally intrusive. It shifts between the impersonal manner of a chronicler and the personal presence of a storyteller, using phrases such as “of which I have spoken” and “which I had better relate connectedly.” The narrator explains local customs, expressions and superstitions for an audience presumed not to know them, often inserting definitions or parenthetical qualifications. This documentary manner lends credibility to the supernatural narrative while preserving the flavour of an orally transmitted legend. The narrator does not openly dispute the villagers’ interpretation of events; instead, fairy belief is presented from within the emotional and cultural logic of the community.

The prose is elaborate, visual and rhythmically expansive. Long, cumulative sentences frequently move through chains of subordinate clauses, appositions and coordinated details. Landscape descriptions unfold panoramically, while supernatural objects are rendered through dense catalogues of colour, costume, movement and ornament. Repetition and parallel construction reinforce both abundance and dread: the carriage is successively gilded, emblazoned and adorned, while the child’s later appearances follow a repeated pattern of smiling, beckoning and vanishing. Shorter sentences are strategically introduced at moments of shock—“Twilight was deepening” or “Molly Ryan never more saw her darling”—giving decisive emotional force to the story’s turning points.

The diction alternates between elevated literary language and strongly regional speech. In the narration, words such as “prophylactic,” “machinations,” “ineffable,” “beleaguering” and “irretrievably” create a formal, learned register. This is contrasted with the Munster-inflected dialogue, represented through phonetic spellings, altered grammar and local vocabulary: “craythurs,” “childhers,” “doore,” “wisha,” “astora” and “mavourneen.” The dialogue conveys social setting, emotional immediacy and oral authenticity. Characters often speak through exclamations, repetitions, blessings and invocations of God, especially in moments of fear. Their Catholic devotional language coexists naturally with pre-Christian fairy lore, revealing a world in which holy water, prayers, rowan trees, horseshoes and house-leek all belong to the same practical system of supernatural defence.

Imagery is dominated by contrasts between beauty and menace, light and darkness, attraction and repulsion. Autumn sunset, purple heath, thinning ash leaves and birdsong create a melancholy pastoral setting, but the lengthening shadow of Lisnavoura turns that beauty ominous. The fairy procession is similarly double-sided. The princess has a sweet, bell-like voice, a captivating smile and jewelled arms, while her servants are diminutive, sharp-featured, fanged and malicious. The enormous white horses and sumptuous gilded carriage evoke aristocratic splendour, yet their exaggerated proportions and unnatural movement make them uncanny. The black attendant, described through grotesque and racialised imagery typical of the period, intensifies this fusion of spectacle and horror. Similes are vivid and concrete: the bog is “level as a lake,” rock formations resemble fortifications, the horses’ manes stream “like so much smoke,” and Billy rises “as lightly as a feather.”

The pacing follows a gradual escalation. The opening lingers over history, geography, poverty and domestic safeguards, establishing both realism and foreboding. The children’s disappearance is then disclosed incrementally: first all three seem missing, then two return, and only afterward is Billy’s loss confirmed. The children’s account temporarily rewinds the chronology and retells the central event in a more continuous, highly visual set piece. After the abduction, the story becomes episodic, recording Billy’s diminishing apparitions over months and years. This deceleration transforms immediate terror into prolonged grief, and the final retrospective passage broadens a single disappearance into a lifelong absence.

Suspense is created largely through foreshadowing and dramatic irony. The profusion of charms around the cabin signals danger before any supernatural event occurs. Sunset, falling leaves, the early barring of doors and the hill’s advancing shadow all mark the approach of a vulnerable threshold between day and night. The adults and readers recognise the danger associated with Lisnavoura before the children do. In the abduction scene, temptation operates through successive distractions: the princess’s beauty masks the hostility around her, and the rolling apples draw the children farther from home without their noticing the distance. Dust then functions as both physical concealment and magical transition, allowing the fairy company to vanish at the exact moment daylight disappears.

Characterisation is economical and archetypal but emotionally effective. Molly Ryan is defined by poverty, maternal vigilance, religious-folkloric fear and helpless grief. Nell initially provides practical reassurance, but her confidence quickly gives way to inherited terror. The younger children are characterised through innocence and sensory response rather than psychological complexity. Billy’s golden hair, blue eyes and simplicity mark him as exceptionally beautiful and therefore especially vulnerable to fairy selection. The supernatural figures are not rounded personalities but embodiments of seduction, caprice and concealed cruelty.

The dominant tone is mournful, ominous and compassionate, with occasional touches of grotesque animation. The story avoids explicit violence; its horror comes from removal, uncertainty and the impossibility of burial. Billy is neither securely alive nor acknowledged as dead, and his fleeting returns deepen rather than relieve the family’s loss. The final image of Lisnavoura seen from afar turns the landscape itself into a memorial. Thus the conclusion shifts from folkloric terror to elegy: the true emotional centre is not the spectacle of fairy abduction, but the enduring pain of a family denied knowledge, recovery and a grave over which to mourn.

generation.response_text:
## The Child of Lisnavoura

Between the brown and melancholy chain of the Ballyhoura hills and that wide tract of bog which, in autumn weather, lies level and dim as a lake of tarnished metal, there runs a road little travelled except by turf-carts, cattle-drovers, and the country people going eastward to Mass. It is not, properly speaking, an ancient road; yet it crosses older ways, whose stones are buried under rushes, and passes more than one grass-grown foundation which the peasantry attribute, according to their humour, either to the Danes, the monks, or the Good People.

To the north may be seen the broken crown of Kilfinnan Castle; westward, beyond the ash woods, the mountains rise in long blue folds; and immediately south of the road stands Lisnavoura.

Lisnavoura is not a high hill. A stranger might pass it without remarking anything more extraordinary than a circular bank near its summit, a few thorn-trees bent all one way by the wind, and certain grey rocks protruding from the heath like the ruined battlements of a fortress. But the inhabitants of that district held it in no light estimation. They would not willingly cross its western slope after sunset, nor cut a branch from its thorns, nor remove even a loose stone from the ring upon its top. Cattle, they said, had been found there in a sweat, though the night was cold; lights had gone round the old enclosure against the course of the sun; and music, ineffably sweet and small, had been heard beneath the ground when no piper, fiddler, or wandering musician was within three miles of the place.

It is necessary to observe that the name is commonly interpreted in the neighbourhood as signifying the Fort of the Yew, although there has been no yew upon it within the memory of man. Some antiquaries, of whom I have spoken elsewhere, maintained that the circular work was military. Old Maurice O’Daly, the schoolmaster, declared it pagan and sacrificial. The poorer people, who troubled themselves little with the disputes of learned men, called it simply the Fairy Rath; and their explanation, if less elaborate, was at least universally understood.

At the foot of this hill, where the bog-road turns beside a stunted rowan-tree and then descends toward the river, stood the cabin of Mary Ryan, a widow with four children. It was a low dwelling, built of stone and yellow clay, with two rooms, a roof of thatch, and a small window looking westward. Behind it were a potato garden, a turf-stack, and a shed for the goat. Before the door a narrow strip of beaten earth sloped to the road, and beyond that road the purple heath ran upward toward Lisnavoura.

Mary’s husband, Michael Ryan, had been killed three years before by the fall of a bank in a quarry. He had left her no property beyond the cabin, the goat, a chest, several iron tools, and a debt at the meal-shop in Kilfinnan. She supported herself and her children by digging potatoes, cutting turf, spinning when flax could be had, and assisting at harvest in the farms below the mountain. Poverty, however, had not made her negligent. The cabin was swept, the hearth-stone whitened, and the children, though patched in every garment, kept as clean as the weather and their occupations permitted.

The eldest, Nell, was nearly thirteen, grave and dark-haired, with much of her mother’s caution. After her came Con, a sturdy boy of nine; little Rose, who had completed her seventh year; and Billy, five years old, light-limbed, blue-eyed, and possessed of such an abundance of curling golden hair that strangers often stopped to look at him. This admiration gave Mary no pleasure.

“Don’t be praising him,” she would say, drawing the child close and making the sign of the cross upon his forehead. “Beauty’s no luck to a poor mother. God stand between him and them that might covet him!”

By “them” she meant the inhabitants of Lisnavoura.

Her precautions were numerous. A horseshoe was nailed above the door; a rowan cross, bound with red thread, hung behind the cradle which Billy had long outgrown; house-leek grew upon the roof; and a little bottle of holy water, renewed every Easter, stood upon the dresser beside a blackened image of the Blessed Virgin. No live coal was lent from the hearth on May Eve. No water used in washing the children’s feet was thrown out after nightfall without the warning cry, “Take care of the water!” And when the wind turned suddenly round the cabin, lifting dust in a narrow pillar, Mary blessed herself and compelled the children to do likewise.

Such observances may appear contradictory to those who imagine that an orthodox devotion must exclude every remnant of elder superstition. In that part of Munster no contradiction was perceived. The priest, the blessed candle, the mountain ash, and the iron tongs were all regarded as forces enlisted upon the same side against powers whose existence was attested by generations of calamity.

Upon the evening when the misfortune occurred, Mary had gone with a neighbour to bring home turf from a distant clamp. The day was in the latter end of October—clear, dry, and touched with that melancholy brightness which belongs only to the decline of the year. The bog pools reflected a pale sky; the fern had turned the colour of rust; the ash leaves, thinned by the first frosts, dropped one by one though scarcely a breath stirred them; and over the western hills the sun hung red and enlarged, as if reluctant to enter the bank of vapour awaiting it.

Before leaving, Mary charged Nell to keep the younger children near the house and bar the door before the shadow of Lisnavoura crossed the road.

“Mind me now,” she said, settling the rope of the creel across her forehead. “The nights are drawing in, and there’s no knowing what does be travelling when decent Christians should be within.”

“Sure I’ll mind them, mammy,” answered Nell. “I have the stirabout to make, and they’ll not go beyond the rowan.”

“You hear that, Con?”

“I do, mammy.”

“And you, Rose?”

“Yes, mammy.”

Billy, who sat on the threshold arranging acorns in a broken saucer, looked up and smiled.

“Come in when Nell bids you, a chuisle,” said Mary, stooping to kiss him. “Don’t be stopping out to see the sun go down.”

She departed along the bog-road, and Nell watched until the turf-creels of the two women had dwindled to dark specks. She then set about her household duties. The three younger children played first beside the turf-stack, building a castle with sods, and afterward crossed the road to gather blackberries from a bramble which had somehow escaped the earlier searchers. Nell called them back twice. They answered readily, and their voices, mingling with the thin evening song of a robin, seemed so near that she ceased to be anxious.

The stirabout, however, was slow in thickening, for the turf upon the fire was damp. Nell knelt to blow the embers, rose to fetch salt, and afterward went into the inner room to bring out four wooden noggins. It could not, she always said, have been more than ten minutes from the last time she heard the children until she came to the door.

Twilight was deepening.

The red light had faded from the bog, and the shadow of Lisnavoura lay across the road. No child was before the cabin.

“Con!” she cried. “Rose! Billy! Come in this minute!”

There was no answer.

She ran to the turf-stack, then round the goat-shed, then across the road. The bramble branches were still trembling, but she could see no one upon the heath. Fear, sudden and hereditary, rose in her throat. She remembered her mother’s tales of voices that answered from the ground and of children found sleeping inside rings of scorched grass.

“Con! Rose! Billy!”

Far down the road came the patter of feet. Two figures emerged from the dusk, running wildly and clinging together. They were Con and Rose. Rose’s apron was torn, Con had lost one shoe, and both were so white and terrified that Nell’s first question died unspoken.

“Where’s Billy?”

Rose screamed.

Con caught Nell’s arm. “Shut the doore! Shut it, for the love of God!”

“Where is he? Where’s Billy?”

“They took him,” said Con, gasping. “The grand people—they took him away to the hill.”

At that instant Mary Ryan appeared upon the road, bent beneath her load of turf. Hearing the cries, she let the creel fall and came running. She looked once at the children, once toward the darkening hill, and knew that the fear of all her poor precautions had at last entered her house.

What the children related, first by fragments and afterward more connectedly, I had better set down in the order in which the thing occurred.

They had strayed farther than they intended, following the blackberry hedge until they came to a green lane branching from the public road. At the entrance of this lane stood an ash-tree under which they had often played; but that evening Billy stopped and listened.

“D’ye hear the bells?” he asked.

Con heard nothing. Rose fancied there was music, very far off and high in the air. Presently all three perceived a sound like the ringing of many silver thimbles, accompanied by a low rushing, though the leaves about them were still.

Then from behind the turn of the lane came two horsemen.

They were no taller than boys of seven, yet their faces were old, sharp, and brown, with pointed chins, glittering eyes, and teeth which showed when they laughed. Their coats, of scarlet cloth, were sewn with gold; each wore enormous riding-boots, a three-cornered hat, and a short sword; and each sat upon a great white horse whose shoulder rose above the children’s heads. The animals were of an unnatural beauty, with red nostrils, milk-coloured eyes, and manes streaming like smoke, although they moved at the solemn pace of a funeral procession.

One rider leaned from his saddle and snapped his fingers close to Rose’s face.

“Out o’ the road, ditch-rat,” he said, grinning.

The other drew his sword half out, causing Con to retreat. The blade shone green, as moonlight shines in deep water.

Behind them came six more white horses, harnessed in silver and drawing a carriage such as had not been seen in that country since the old lords left their houses to ruin. It was high, narrow, and old-fashioned, painted a lustrous blue and enriched upon every panel with golden birds, stars, crowns, and flowers. Small lamps burned at its four corners, though evening was not yet wholly gone; long silken tassels swung from the roof; the wheels, scarlet at the spokes and gilt at the rims, turned without sound over stone or rut; and upon the hammercloth behind sat two dwarf servants in green livery, their little withered faces maliciously attentive.

There were two ladies within.

The elder, who occupied the farther corner, was wrapped in black. A veil descended from a pointed cap and concealed her features to the mouth; but the visible mouth was thin and grey, and her long hands, folded upon her lap, were covered with dark rings. She neither moved nor spoke. The nearer lady leaned from the open window.

The children could afterward describe every jewel she wore, yet none could agree upon the colour of her dress. To Con it seemed crimson, to Rose green as young leaves, and Nell declared that Billy, at one of his later appearances, had whispered—or seemed about to whisper—that it was white. Her hair was bright brown, braided with pearls; her arms were bare to the elbow and covered with bracelets; and her face had such sweetness that even Rose, while recounting the horror, began to cry because she could not forget its beauty.

“What pretty little craythurs!” said the lady, in a voice clear and delicate as a bell heard across frost. “And whose children may ye be?”

Con remembered his mother’s warnings and did not answer.

The dwarf upon the leading horse made a hideous grimace. “No manners,” he said. “Bog-bred and bare-legged.”

The lady reproved him with a smile and turned again to the children.

“Will none of ye speak to me?”

“We’re Mary Ryan’s,” said Rose.

“And which is the youngest?”

Billy stepped forward before Con could restrain him.

“I am, ma’am.”

The lady’s smile brightened. “And what is your name, golden head?”

“Billy Ryan.”

“Come nearer, Billy Ryan. I have something for you.”

She held out a small red apple. Its skin was so polished that it caught the last light and seemed luminous from within. Billy approached. Con seized the back of his coat, but one of the mounted dwarfs struck Con’s fingers with his riding-switch. The pain was so sharp that he released his hold.

The lady touched Billy under the chin.

“A handsome child,” she said.

At this the veiled woman in the carriage turned her head. Though her eyes could not be seen, the children felt her gaze pass over Billy slowly, as a cold shadow passes across grass.

“Too pale,” she murmured.

“He will redden with us,” replied the beautiful lady.

Then she took Billy by both hands. He rose from the ground as lightly as a feather lifted by an upward draught, passed through the carriage window without striking the frame, and settled upon her lap. He did not cry out. He looked surprised, but happy, and suffered her to place the apple between his hands.

Con ran at the carriage. The dwarf servants hissed and showed their narrow teeth. One kicked at him with a buckled shoe, while another uncoiled a whip whose lash moved of itself upon the road like a black worm.

“Give him back!” Con shouted. “That’s our Billy!”

The lady laughed—not loudly, nor, as Rose insisted, unkindly.

“Why, certainly. He shall go home. Follow us a little way, and I will set him down where the road is smooth.”

The carriage moved on.

Con and Rose followed, calling to Billy. The white horses did not appear to quicken their pace, yet the children were obliged to run. Billy looked from the window, smiling, with the apple pressed against his breast. Whenever Con drew near the rear wheel, one of the dwarfs threatened him; and whenever Rose began to wail, the beautiful lady leaned out and spoke soothingly.

“Do not cry, little sister. See what I have for you.”

She scattered three apples upon the road. They rolled ahead of the children, bright and red in the grey twilight. Rose, thinking perhaps that the carriage would stop while she gathered them, stooped and caught one. The moment she touched it, another appeared farther on.

Again and again the lady threw the fruit, sometimes red, sometimes yellow, sometimes of a deep purple colour such as no natural apple bears. The children pursued them, and by this innocent machination were drawn onward without considering the distance. They passed the rowan-tree, the abandoned limekiln, and the stream where the road forks. Before them Lisnavoura grew black against a strip of dying gold.

At the crossroads Con at last overtook the carriage and caught the brass handle behind. It was cold enough to burn his palm.

“Billy!” he cried.

Billy turned. For the first time his smile faded. He put out his hands and seemed about to spring down.

The veiled woman bent forward and enclosed him in her long arms.

At once a whirlwind arose in the centre of the road. Dust, dead leaves, straws, and little stones spun upward in a roaring column. The horses screamed; the lamps of the carriage shone blue through the murk; and the dwarfs’ laughter came from every side—above, below, behind the children, and apparently from within the ground itself.

Con was flung into the ditch. Rose fell upon her knees and covered her face.

The wind ceased.

The road was empty. The last daylight had gone, and from the thorn-ring upon Lisnavoura there came, or they imagined there came, the faint chiming of bells.

Mary did not wait for the conclusion. With Nell carrying the holy-water bottle and Con holding a lighted wisp of straw, she ran to the crossroads. Neighbours joined them: old men with lanterns, women with shawls thrown over their heads, boys carrying pitchforks and spades. They searched every ditch and drain. They called Billy’s name along the road, through the heather, and beneath the thorn-trees of the rath. Mary would have entered the ring itself, but the others restrained her, not from cowardice, as some afterward said, but because a person who invades such a place in anger may be lost along with the one sought.

“Billy, astora!” she cried until her voice broke. “Billy, mavourneen, answer your poor mammy!”

No answer came.

At midnight Father Maher arrived from Kilfinnan. He brought a stole, a crucifix, and holy water, and went farther upon the hill than any of the others dared to go. What prayers he recited there were not repeated; but near dawn he returned, pale and exhausted, and said only that the child was not to be found by ordinary searching.

For nine days Mary kept the door unbarred and food upon the table. For nine nights a candle burned in the western window. Fairy doctors were consulted from three counties. One prescribed foxglove gathered with the left hand; another directed that Billy’s clothes should be burned at the crossroads; a third listened at the hearth with his ear to the floor and declared that the child was living beneath running water. Their ceremonies, though expensive to a woman who could ill afford them, produced nothing.

Winter entered the valley. Rain loosened the thatch, snow covered the rath, and the bog became impassable. Still Mary looked up whenever the latch stirred.

Toward the end of January, Rose awoke after midnight and saw Billy standing outside the window.

The moon was bright, and she knew him at once. He wore the same little grey coat in which he had disappeared; his golden hair was neatly curled; his cheeks were rosy; and he smiled as though he had returned from a pleasant visit. He raised one finger and beckoned.

Rose sprang from the bed, calling his name. Before her feet touched the floor, he was gone.

Tracks were found beneath the window next morning—small footprints upon the frozen earth. They led toward Lisnavoura and ended where the road began.

Thereafter he appeared at uncertain intervals. Nell saw him at the cabin door in March, holding a bunch of primroses. Con saw him beside the stream on a summer evening. In each instance Billy smiled and beckoned, but did not speak; and if the witness advanced, called aloud, or made the sign of the cross, he vanished—not gradually, like a figure retiring into mist, but instantaneously, as the reflection of a face leaves dark water when the light is removed.

Mary never saw him.

This was the sharpest point of her affliction. Strangers might have supposed that the children imagined these visitations out of grief; but no argument could console the mother, who believed that Billy was permitted to approach the house, though some fairy prohibition kept him from her sight.

“Why wouldn’t he show himself to me?” she would say. “Didn’t I carry him? Didn’t I rear him? Ah, God help me, maybe he comes when I’m sleeping, and stands over me, the poor innocent, and I not knowing!”

As the months passed, the appearances became rarer. The grey coat looked worn. The primroses were replaced by withered leaves. Once Con saw marks like bruises around Billy’s wrists; and once Rose heard, after he vanished, a sound beneath the road resembling a child sobbing at a great distance.

Nearly a year and a half had elapsed when the last occurrence took place.

It was early spring, before dawn, and the weather bitterly cold. The family slept in the inner room, the fire in the kitchen having sunk to a red spark among the ashes. Nell, who had become a light sleeper, awoke to a faint scraping. At first she thought the goat had entered; then she saw the red gleam of the embers brighten, as if someone knelt before them.

She rose and looked through the open doorway.

A child sat upon the hearth.

He was barefoot and dressed in rags. His hair, once golden, hung in damp, colourless locks; his face was narrow and white; and his hands, stretched above the dying fire, were so thin that the light shone between the bones of the fingers. Upon the settle beside him lay a crust of bread which he had taken from the table, and he ate it ravenously, though without making the least sound.

Nell knew him.

“Billy,” she whispered.

He looked round.

There was no smile now. His eyes were large with hunger and fear. For one suspended moment brother and sister gazed at one another across the poor room—the dresser, the iron pot, the bottle of holy water, the rowan cross, all those familiar and insufficient safeguards.

Then Nell cried, “Mammy! Mammy, he’s here!”

Billy leaped up. She reached him before he gained the door and caught a fold of his ragged coat. The cloth came away in her hand, cold and wet as something taken from a grave. He passed over the threshold.

Mary ran after him barefoot, followed by all the children. The sky was beginning to whiten above the eastern hills. They saw Billy upon the road, moving with extraordinary swiftness, though his feet appeared scarcely to touch the ground.

“Stop, astora!” Mary cried. “Only stop till I bless you!”

He paused at the rowan-tree.

For the first and last time since his abduction, mother and child looked upon one another. Billy lifted both arms toward her. Whether he spoke, none could say. Mary believed she heard the word “Mammy,” but the others heard only the wind.

A grey light flowed over Lisnavoura. Billy became indistinct in it, wavered like a figure seen through rain, and disappeared.

They found no footprints, though the roadside mud was soft. The fragment of cloth remained in Nell’s hand until sunrise, when it crumbled into a reddish dust and was blown about the floor.

Billy Ryan was never seen again.

Father Maher afterward performed prayers at the cabin and upon the road; another priest, younger and less tolerant of the old beliefs, urged Mary to regard the visions as delusions born of sorrow. She submitted to his instruction, as a devout woman should, but in her heart nothing was altered. She continued for many years to place a portion of bread beside the fire on the anniversary of Billy’s return, and she never allowed the door to be wholly fastened before dawn in spring.

The children grew. Nell married a farmer near Mitchelstown; Con went to sea; Rose entered service in Cork. Mary remained in the cabin until age bent her almost double and whitened her hair. Those who visited her found her gentle, rational, and little inclined to recount the marvel; but if a child with fair curls passed the door at twilight, she would rise suddenly and follow it with her eyes until it was lost from view.

She died without certainty and was buried beside her husband. There was no smaller grave between them.

The cabin has since fallen. Nettles grow within its walls, and the rowan-tree was split by lightning many winters ago. Yet the road remains, the crossroads remain, and above them Lisnavoura keeps its ancient circle of thorns and stones. Travellers who know nothing of Mary Ryan may admire, on a clear autumn evening, the purple heath, the westward mountains, and the last red brightness resting upon the bog; but the older people hurry their steps when the hill’s shadow reaches across the road.

For they remember that beauty came from Lisnavoura in a gilded carriage, with lamps and music and apples shining in the dusk; and that a poor woman’s child went away smiling among its splendours, to return only once, barefoot, starving, and afraid.

The Bell at the Bottom of the Lake

Every morning at six, the bell beneath Lake Arlen rang once.

It was not loud. People standing on the shore heard only a low bronze note passing through the water, but in the village houses the cups trembled in their cupboards, windowpanes hummed, and sleeping dogs lifted their heads.

No one knew why the bell rang.

The oldest villagers said it belonged to a church drowned when the valley was flooded. The oldest maps, however, showed no church in the valley—only farms, orchards, and a narrow road that followed the vanished river north.

Some claimed the bell was rung by currents. Others blamed the shifting of the lakebed. Children whispered that a drowned priest pulled the rope, tolling once each morning for the soul he had failed to save.

Mara Vale did not believe any of these stories.

She maintained the village clocks.

There were seventy-three of them: wall clocks, grandfather clocks, carriage clocks, a brass marine chronometer in the mayor’s office, and the large white clock in the railway station, though no train had stopped there for twenty years. Mara wound, cleaned, and repaired them all. She knew that every mystery had a mechanism. What people called magic was often just a spring hidden behind a face.

The underwater bell, she believed, had a mechanism too.

Her father had believed otherwise.

“The lake keeps time,” he used to say. “It doesn’t measure it. There’s a difference.”

He disappeared on Lake Arlen when Mara was twelve. His boat was found drifting near the northern cliffs, with one oar missing and the other laid neatly across the seat. His coat, lunch tin, and pocket watch were still inside. The watch had stopped at six in the morning.

For years, Mara refused to go near the shore.

Then, on the first day of autumn in her thirty-fourth year, the bell rang twice.

The first note came at six, as always.

The second followed three seconds later.

Across the village, people woke and waited in frightened silence. The sound faded through the foundations of their homes.

That afternoon, a shepherd found a dead swan on the eastern bank. The next day, milk soured before noon. By evening, rumors had multiplied like flies.

Mara spent the day repairing Mrs. Pell’s mantel clock, which had not chimed correctly since her husband’s funeral.

“Two bells,” Mrs. Pell said, watching Mara fit a pin into the striking mechanism. “It means the lake wants another sacrifice.”

“The lake doesn’t want anything.”

“That’s what your father said before it took him.”

Mara’s hand slipped. The pin scratched the brass plate.

“My father said the lake kept time.”

Mrs. Pell’s lined face softened. “Did he?”

“Yes.”

“I remember him saying many things.”

“So do I.”

Mara closed the clock case and wound it. At four, the little clock chimed four clear notes.

That night, someone knocked on Mara’s door.

Outside stood a boy of about ten, barefoot despite the cold. His dark hair dripped water onto the step.

“Are you the clock mender?” he asked.

“Who are you?”

“Eli.”

“Where are your shoes?”

The boy looked down, as if surprised by his bare feet. “I lost them.”

“In the rain?”

“It isn’t raining.”

Mara glanced past him. The lane was dry beneath the moon.

“Where do you live?”

Eli pointed toward the lake.

A chill moved through her, but she did not believe in ghosts. Children ran away. Children became confused. Children told strange stories when they were afraid.

She let him inside, wrapped him in a blanket, and put a kettle on the stove.

“Your family will be worried.”

“They’re waiting.”

“Where?”

“Below.”

The kettle began to whisper.

Mara sat opposite him. “Did someone tell you to come here?”

“Yes.”

“Who?”

“Your father.”

The kettle screamed.

Mara stood so abruptly that her chair fell backward.

The boy watched her without blinking.

“My father is dead.”

“No,” Eli said. “He’s late.”

Mara ordered him to stay where he was and hurried next door to fetch Constable Rusk. She was gone less than five minutes. When she returned, the blanket lay folded on the chair.

The back door was bolted from within. The front door had been in her sight as she crossed the lane.

On the table, in a small puddle of lake water, rested a brass key.

Rusk examined it beneath the lamp.

“Old,” he said.

“I can see that.”

“Could belong to a cabinet. Maybe a music box.”

“The boy left it.”

“What boy?”

Mara stared at him.

Rusk rubbed his mustache. “You said no one was here when you returned.”

“He was here before.”

“Of course.”

“You don’t believe me.”

“I believe you saw someone.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“No,” he admitted. “It isn’t.”

At six the next morning, the bell rang three times.

By sunrise, half the village had gathered at the shore. The lake lay smooth and gray, untouched by wind. Each ring had sent a perfect circle across its surface. The last ripples were only just disappearing.

Mayor Cale called an emergency meeting in the town hall. He spoke of safety, investigation, and the importance of avoiding panic. Everyone panicked immediately.

The fishermen refused to launch their boats. The school closed. Mrs. Pell began hanging iron nails over windows. Old Amos Reed walked through the streets shouting that the drowned valley was rising.

Mara returned to her workshop and placed the brass key under a magnifying lens.

On its shaft she found three tiny letters: A.V.C.

Arlen Valley Clockworks.

She knew the name. Long before the valley was flooded, the company had made tower clocks. Only a few survived, including one in the provincial museum. Mara had seen it as an apprentice: a massive iron mechanism whose central wheel was taller than she was.

According to the museum plaque, the company factory had stood somewhere near the old river.

Somewhere beneath Lake Arlen.

Mara spent the afternoon in the municipal archive. At the bottom of a dust-coated drawer, she found construction plans for the dam. Most buildings in the valley had been demolished before flooding, but one structure had been left intact: the Arlen Valley Clockworks factory.

A red handwritten note in the margin explained why.

FOUNDATIONS TOO DEEP. DEMOLITION UNSAFE. MACHINERY REMOVED.

A second note had been added below.

LOWER CHAMBER SEALED.

Mara copied the coordinates.

At dusk, she went to the boathouse once owned by her father. The door resisted, swollen by years of damp, before opening with a groan.

His small blue boat remained inside.

Mara ran her hand along its peeling side. Dust covered the benches, but the old anchor was there, along with rope, two oars, and a hand-cranked depth line. On a shelf she found her father’s diving lantern, sealed in thick glass.

Beneath it was a notebook.

Most pages contained sketches of fishing hooks and weather observations. Near the end, his handwriting grew hurried.

Bell rang at 5:57. Village clocks showed 6:00.

Next day: bell at 5:54. Clocks still 6:00.

It isn’t following the clocks. They are following it.

On the final page, he had drawn a circle divided into gear teeth. Beneath it were the words:

If it stops, time returns to the valley.

Mara read the sentence until darkness filled the boathouse.

At six the next morning, the bell rang four times.

Mara was already on the lake.

Constable Rusk sat in the bow, pale and unhappy. Mara had told him only that she had discovered the possible location of the bell. He brought grappling hooks, a coil of rope, and an old diving suit from the fire station.

“Your plan,” he said, “is terrible.”

“You volunteered.”

“I volunteered to prevent you from going alone.”

“That was kind.”

“It was administrative.”

Mist covered the water. Mara rowed north, counting strokes. When the depth line showed thirty fathoms, she adjusted their course toward the cliffs.

The coordinates led them to a spot where the lake darkened from silver to black.

Rusk peered over the side. “How far down?”

“Forty feet to the factory roof. Maybe sixty to the lower chamber.”

“I dislike every word in that sentence.”

Mara fastened the diving suit. It was stiff, patched, and smelled of rubber. A hose connected the helmet to a hand pump in the boat.

“If I pull twice, give me more air. Three times means pull me up.”

“And four?”

“Four means I’ve forgotten the instructions.”

“Mara.”

She looked at him.

“Come back up.”

She nodded, put on the helmet, and descended.

The cold struck first.

Then came the silence.

The lake closed above her in layers of green and gray. Rusk and the boat vanished. Only the rope remained, trembling beside her.

The factory roof emerged from the darkness like the deck of a sunken ship. Chimneys leaned at impossible angles. Pale fish drifted through broken windows.

Mara landed in the courtyard. Silt rose around her boots.

An iron sign lay half buried near the entrance:

ARLEN VALLEY CLOCKWORKS  
WE MAKE THE HOURS HONEST

She entered.

Worktables stood in long rows. Tools still hung from hooks, though the construction note had claimed the machinery was removed. On one table rested dozens of unfinished clock faces, each without hands.

Mara’s lantern swept across the walls.

Someone had drawn arrows in white chalk.

They pointed toward a stairwell.

The chalk should have dissolved decades ago.

She followed.

At the bottom of the stairs, she found a steel door. Its keyhole was bright, untouched by rust.

Mara removed the brass key from the pouch at her belt.

It turned easily.

The lower chamber was dry.

Water rolled from her suit as she stepped across the threshold. Behind her, the open doorway remained filled with lake water, held back by nothing she could see. It trembled like glass.

Mara removed her helmet.

A ticking filled the chamber.

It came from thousands of clocks.

They covered the walls from floor to ceiling. Clocks made of oak, gold, tin, bone, porcelain, and stone. Watches hung from the ceiling on chains. Pendulums swung in perfect unison.

All showed six o’clock.

At the center stood the bell.

It was smaller than Mara expected, no larger than a washbasin. Green corrosion coated its bronze sides. No rope hung from it. Instead, it formed part of an enormous clock mechanism sunk into the floor.

Iron gears turned beneath glass panels. Each rotation pulled back a hammer by one notch.

The hammer was now five notches from the bell.

“Mara.”

She froze.

Her father stepped out from behind the mechanism.

He looked exactly as he had on the morning he vanished. Brown coat. Muddy boots. Gray beginning at his temples. His face was tired but alive.

Mara could not speak.

He smiled uncertainly. “You grew up.”

She crossed the room and struck him in the chest.

He staggered.

“You left me,” she said.

“I know.”

“You were gone twenty-two years.”

“Not for me.”

“How long?”

He looked at the clocks. “A day. Perhaps two.”

She hit him again, but this time her fist remained pressed to his coat. He covered her hand with his.

“I tried to come back.”

“You left your watch.”

“It stopped when I entered.”

“Why are you here?”

“To keep the mechanism running.”

Mara looked at the gears. “What does it do?”

Her father led her to the glass floor.

Deep below, beneath the gears, the old valley lay in sunlight.

She saw orchards in bloom. Cattle moved through green fields. Smoke curled from chimneys. People walked along the vanished road, unaware of the lake above them.

“That isn’t possible,” Mara whispered.

“No.”

“Are they ghosts?”

“I don’t know.”

A horse-drawn cart passed beneath their feet. Its driver raised a hand to someone beyond view.

Her father pointed to the largest gear. Five teeth were broken.

“The clockworks owner built this before the flood. He thought time was like water—that it could be dammed, diverted, preserved. When the valley was drowned, the mechanism trapped its final morning.”

“And the bell?”

“Keeps the moment sealed. One ring each day resets everything below. Sunrise begins again. The same conversations, the same journeys, the same birds crossing the same sky.”

Mara thought of the boy dripping water onto her floor.

“Eli.”

Her father’s face changed.

“You saw him?”

“He brought me the key.”

“He’s the owner’s son. He knows more than the others. Children sometimes notice repetition. He has been trying to escape for decades.”

“Why did the bell ring twice?”

“The mechanism is failing. Each broken tooth makes the hammer strike again. Tomorrow it will ring five times. Then six. When the final gear breaks, all the years held outside the valley will fall in at once.”

“What will happen?”

“To the people below? They will age eighty years in a second.”

“And the village?”

“The same force may pull your time backward. Your homes, your families—everything built since the flood could vanish.”

Mara stared at the mechanism.

“How do we repair it?”

“We don’t.”

“You repaired clocks.”

“I maintained a prison.”

The words echoed among the ticking.

Her father touched the bell. “I thought keeping it running would protect everyone. Each day I told myself I needed one more day to understand it. But the machine takes years from those outside and gives them here. It took twenty-two from you.”

“Then stop it.”

“I can’t. Someone from outside must choose. The clock doesn’t recognize me anymore.”

Mara moved toward the main lever. It was red, polished by her father’s hand.

A small brass plate bore two words:

RELEASE / RETAIN

“What happens if I release it?”

“The valley returns to time. The lake remains. The people below die as they should have died long ago. The village above continues.”

“And you?”

“I continue too.”

“For how long?”

He did not answer.

She understood.

“No.”

“Mara.”

“No. Come with me.”

“I can’t cross the water. I tried.”

“Then I’ll find another way.”

“The hammer has already moved.”

The gears clanked.

Four notches remained.

All around them, the clocks ticked faster.

Through the glass floor, sunlight flickered. The trapped villagers repeated tiny movements: a woman opened a gate, a man lifted a sack, a child ran after a hoop.

Eli stood in the road.

Unlike the others, he looked up.

He could see her.

He raised one hand and pressed it to the invisible ceiling of his world.

Mara knelt above him.

Her father said, “He is asking you to let the morning end.”

Mara remembered waking every day to the bell. She remembered her father’s empty chair, his untouched tools, and the villagers lowering their voices whenever she entered a room. For years she had wished that one morning could be undone.

But a morning without an evening was not life.

It was only a clock with painted hands.

She stood and gripped the lever.

“Will it hurt?”

“For them? No.”

“For you?”

Her father smiled. “I’ve missed you longer than I knew.”

The hammer moved another notch.

Mara pulled the lever to RELEASE.

The ticking stopped.

For one vast second, every clock in the chamber showed a different time.

Then the hands began to turn.

Some raced forward. Others backward. Pendulums swung wildly. Watch springs snapped with sharp metallic cries.

Below the glass, the valley’s sun crossed the sky.

Day became night, then day again. Seasons rippled over the fields. Leaves burned gold and vanished. Snow covered the road. Houses sagged. Orchards grew wild.

The people were gone.

Eli remained for one moment longer than the rest. He stood beneath falling snow, smiling up at Mara.

Then he vanished too.

The great mechanism split down the center.

Water burst through the doorway.

Her father pushed the diving helmet into her arms.

“Go.”

She tried to hold him, but water struck them apart. The chamber filled with thunder. Clocks tore from the walls and spun through the flood.

Mara forced on the helmet. The air hose pulled tight.

Through the churning water, she saw her father beside the bell. He raised his hand.

Not goodbye, she decided.

Just a wave from one shore to another.

The rope jerked upward. Rusk was pulling.

The factory collapsed beneath her.

For a few terrible seconds she was trapped in black silt. Then she rose through broken beams and clouds of silver bubbles. Her lungs burned. The hose bucked. Somewhere below, the bell began to fall.

It rang once.

The note moved through Mara’s bones.

Then the lake released her.

Rusk hauled her into the boat. The diving helmet rolled against the oars. Mara lay gasping while waves struck the hull.

The mist had disappeared.

On the northern shore, something extraordinary was happening. The lake had withdrawn several yards, exposing a strip of old road. Cracked stones gleamed in the morning sun.

Along the road stood a single milestone.

Rusk helped Mara sit up.

“What happened?”

“I stopped a clock.”

He waited for more.

She had nothing else she could say.

They returned to the village shortly before noon. Everyone crowded around them, asking about the bell, the waves, and the road.

Mayor Cale demanded an official explanation.

Mara told him the truth.

He wrote down “submerged mechanical failure.”

That evening, the villagers stayed awake, waiting for the next morning. Some gathered by the shore. Others sat in kitchens with lamps burning. Mrs. Pell held her husband’s repaired mantel clock on her knees.

Mara waited alone in her workshop.

At five fifty-nine, every clock in the village began to tick.

At six, there was no bell.

No cups trembled. No windows hummed. The lake remained silent.

People looked at one another, uncertain what to do with a morning that had not been announced.

Then Mrs. Pell’s mantel clock chimed.

Another clock answered from across the lane. Then another, and another, until the village filled with mismatched ringing—fast clocks, slow clocks, bright clocks, cracked clocks, each keeping its own imperfect hour.

Mara opened her father’s pocket watch.

It had rested motionless in her drawer for twenty-two years.

The second hand moved.

Once.

Twice.

Then steadily onward.

In the weeks that followed, the exposed road became a place where villagers left flowers. No one agreed on what had happened beneath the lake, but the stories changed. They no longer spoke of a drowned priest or a hungry water spirit. They spoke of a hidden valley that had finally reached evening.

Mara returned to repairing clocks.

She no longer made them all agree.

When Mayor Cale complained that the town hall clock ran thirty seconds behind the station clock, Mara told him, “They have different distances to travel.”

He did not understand, but he stopped complaining.

Years later, when Mara’s hair had begun to gray, a girl brought a broken music box to the workshop. Inside, beneath the cylinder, Mara found the maker’s mark of Arlen Valley Clockworks.

A.V.C.

The girl watched as Mara cleaned the gears.

“Can you fix anything?” she asked.

“No.”

“Most things?”

“Some.”

“What do you do when you can’t fix something?”

Mara considered the question.

Outside, Lake Arlen shone beneath the afternoon sun. Wind moved over its surface, breaking the light into a thousand pieces. There had been no bell for many years.

“You let it change,” she said.

She wound the music box and set it on the table.

For a moment, nothing happened.

Then the cylinder turned, the teeth caught, and a simple melody filled the room. It was not quite in tune. One note came late, and another trembled longer than it should.

Mara listened until the last note faded.

The clock on the wall ticked on, honest and imperfect, carrying them all toward evening.
